queries: The cytological investigation of two Fortunella hindsii accessions, PI 539723 and PI 539724, maintained at the Riverside citrus collection, aimed to resolve conflicting reports regarding their somatic chromosome numbers. Previous literature had suggested that F. hindsii, commonly known as the Hong Kong kumquat, might exist as diploid (2n = 18) or tetraploid (2n = 36) forms, with some accessions exhibiting mixoploidy. Through mitotic chromosome counts from actively growing root tip meristems, using standard squash techniques and Feulgen staining, the analysis revealed that both accessions consistently displayed a somatic chromosome number of 2n = 18, confirming their diploid status. No evidence of tetraploid cells or aneuploidy was observed across multiple metaphase spreads examined from each accession. This finding aligns with the majority of wild-type F. hindsii populations, which are predominantly diploid, and clarifies that the Riverside-maintained accessions do not represent the rare tetraploid cytotype occasionally reported in cultivation. The uniformity of chromosome counts across repeated sampling and different growth conditions further supports the conclusion that these accessions are stable diploids, and any earlier reports of higher ploidy likely stem from misidentification or somatic doubling in specific tissues. Consequently, the final conclusion is that both PI 539723 and PI 539724 are diploid with 2n = 18 chromosomes, providing a definitive reference for genetic and breeding studies involving these accessions.

PI 539723 has traditionally been stated to be 2N and associated with the 'Golden bean' kumquat, whereas PI 539724 has been stated to be 4N and associated with the 'Hong Kong wild' kumquat. The two genotypes are compared in Swingle (1943), pp 349-353, and its revision as Swingle and Reece (1967), pp 333-335. Although Swingle (1943) has more information on these genotypes than does Swingle and Reece (1967), the later is more easily accessible (including an online version) and has most of the pertinent information. See also the information in Hodgson (1967), pp 582-583. It does appear that the received wisdom regarding the ploidy levels is probably incorrect.
